msDesc.head: Three taẕkīrahs (literary chronicles), two in Persian and one in Urdu.

msContents.summary: This composite manuscript contains three (taẕkīrah) literary chronicles in Persian and Urdu. The similar paper but slightly different hands and layouts suggest that a different stationer-copyist collectively prepared the volume. The scribe Shaykh ʿAbd al-Karīm completed the first text, Ikhlāṣ Chand's Hamīshah Bahār (Eternal Spring), in 1136. The volume also contains Ḥazīn's Taz̲kirah-'i Muʿāṣirīn (Chronicle of Contemporaries), and Qā'im's Makhzan-i Nikāt (Treasury of Witticisms).

supportDesc.support: Very thin wove paper probably manufactured in Europe, with an illegible embossed mill or stationer's mark on the second right flyleaf.
supportDesc.extent:
264 folios, 2 flyleaves (ff. ii + 130 + 70 + 64 [=264]). Note that the binder hinged the final quire of the textblock to the pastedown, so while the volume ends with a blank page, it technically lacks any right flyleaves.

supportDesc.foliation: Modern foliation in Hindu-Arabic numerals at the upper right corners in pencil.
supportDesc.collation: Quaternions throughout, 33IV(264). Catchwords on the b sides throughout most of the volume; however, the third title lacks many.

physDesc.additions: Bookplates: Left paste-down: Bibliotheca Lindesiana with shelfmark 2/J, and Bland MSS No. 543, with the name and number crossed out and Persian and 323 written aside.

binding.p: Unsupported sewing at two stations, edges trimmed, with twined chevron headbands. Bound in a hybrid British-Indian style, tight-backed in full smooth red goatskin leather over pasteboards, in a type III binding (without flap as per Déroche), squares along the edges, defined joints, and one trimmmed headcap present at tail, with the upper one now missing. A bifolium tipped onto the right side of the textblock provides the first flyleaves, with the excess width adhered as a hinge over top.

decoNote.p: Boards decorated with stamped paper onlay scalloped central mandorlas and corners, with detached pendants featuring large floral scrollwork designs, joined by a criss-crossed single ruled line in yellow, and bounded by the same around the perimetres of the boards. Paper label on the spine, now faded. Titles of the three texts are inscribed directly on the spine in black ink.

binding.condition: Fair condition. Exterior binding abraded. White pigment, probably lead, appears to be shifting gray.

history.origin: Probably completed in the Indian subcontinent; dated to after 3 Ṣafar 1225 AH (10 March 1810 CE), mentioned in the colophon of the first work on folio 129a).

provenance.p: Later acquired by scholar Nathaniel Bland (1803–1865), after whose death London bookseller Bernard Quaritch (1819–1899) sold his oriental manuscripts to Alexander Lindsay, 25th Earl of Crawford (1812–1880) in 1866.

history.provenance: Purchased by Enriqueta Rylands (1843–1908) in 1901 from James Ludovic Lindsay, 26th Earl of Crawford (1847–1913).

acquisition.p: Bequeathed by Enriqueta Rylands (1843–1908) in 1908 to the John Rylands Library.

source.p: Bibliographical description based on an index created by Reza Navabpour circa 1993, derived from a manuscript catalogue by Michael Kerney, circa 1890s and his Bibliotheca Lindesiana, Hand-list of Oriental Manuscripts: Arabic, Persian, Turkish, 1898.
Revised and expanded by James White in 2018 with reference to the manuscript in hand.
Further amended and enhanced by Jake Benson in 2021, with reference to the volume.

availability.p: The manuscript is available for consultation by any accredited reader, see Becoming a Reader for details. Please contact uml.special-collections@manchester.ac.uk for further information on the availability of this manuscript.

summary.seg: Author Kishan Chand Ikhlāṣ (ca. 1683–1748) compiled his chronicle Hamīshah Bahār (Eternal Spring), which relates accounts of nearly 200 Mughal-era Persian poets. He completed the work in his native Shāhjahānābād (Dehli) in 1136 AH (1723–1724 CE), indicated by a chronogram in the title. Shaykh ʿAbd al-Karīm completed this manuscript on 3 Ṣafar 1225 AH (10 March 1810 CE).

summary.seg: While Muḥammad ʿAlī Ḥazīn (1691-1766) commences his Taz̲kirah-'i Muʿāṣirīn (Chronicle of Contemporaries) on his birthday in Rabī‘ I 1103 (Nov–Dec. 1691 CE) he completed it in nine days in 1165 AH (1751–1752 CE). He completed the work under durress and lacked sources to cite for many entires, so he relied upon his own prodigious memory and eyewitness accounts when compiling this account. He divided it into two parts (Farqah), with twenty accounts of religious scholars who wrote poetry and eighty memoirs of professional poets whome he knew personally. The invaluable work thus records many names not recounted in prior sources.

summary.seg: Muḥammad Qiyām al-Dīn Qāʼim Chāndpūrī (ca. 1722–1793) completed his chronicle of Hindustani Rekhta poetry, Makhzan-i Nikāt (Treasury of Witticisms) in 1168 AH (1755 CE), as indicated by a chronogram from the title. He finished it a few years after his contemporaries Mīr Taqī Mīr and Fatḥ ‘Alī Ḥusaynī completed their chronicles Nikāt al-Shu‘arā (Witticisms of Poets) and Tazkirah-i Rikhtah-Gūyān (Chronicle of Rekhta Reciters) completed their works in 1752. Unlike those authors, who arranged their works alphabetically, he chose a chronological format. This manuscript regrettably abruptly ends about three-quarters of the way through, in a section in which the author relates his own original poetic compositions.
